hook_clip: Here's how to reverse engineer Rocketlane from a written spec. Claude passed all twenty-eight checks, and found eighteen gaps in my spec.
outro_clip: The full spec is free at personal software factory dot com. If you build it, tell me what broke. I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.

scenes.text: We gave Claude one Markdown file. It copies the part of Rocketlane a small team actually needs for client onboarding. Templates with a checklist for every stage. One project per client, copied from a template. Handoffs that pass the project to a new owner, with a note. And a read-only link that shows the client their progress.

The core rule is the stage gate. Every client moves through four stages: kickoff, setup, training and live. A project can only leave a stage when every task in it is done, or skipped with a reason. Bluebird is in setup, with two tasks still open. So the handoff to training is refused, and the app names the open tasks.
cues: every task in it is done

scenes.text: Claude built it in four phases, one prompt each. The foundation, with people, templates and sign-in. Projects, checklists and stage gates. Notifications, the daily digest, and projects on hold. Then the client link, handoffs and CSV export. After every phase, the acceptance checks ran in a real browser, from fresh seed data.

Here's what it built. The board shows every client by stage, with three in progress and four overdue tasks. Bluebird's project page shows the setup checklist, with training locked until setup is done. A new project previews all six tasks and their due dates. Each morning, a digest lists what's overdue. And the client's link shows only shared tasks, never internal ones.
In one final run, on a fresh database, all twenty-eight checks passed, along with one hundred and nineteen automated tests.

But the more useful result is what broke. The build exposed eighteen gaps in the spec. Places where Claude had to guess. A live project still counted as active, so its owner could never be deactivated. Nothing stopped an admin deactivating the last admin. And digest items named only the client, which is ambiguous once a client has two projects. Every gap is now fixed in the spec.

Passing every check isn't the same as production-ready. We didn't test production sign-in, real email delivery, the hourly job on a real scheduler, or hosting. Those are yours to check before your team relies on it.

So is it worth building? Rocketlane's Standard plan is forty-nine dollars per team member per month, billed annually, with a minimum of five. That's at least two thousand nine hundred and forty dollars a year. Premium is sixty-nine. If clients need to log in and tick off their own tasks, or you bill for time, buy Rocketlane. If you run the same checklist for a few clients a month, build it.
Everything is in one file. The data model, eighteen rules, seed data, four phase prompts, and all twenty-eight checks, with the eighteen fixes already in.
